It seems like most people have heard of ARMA, but only by it's increasingly undeserved reputation of being a resource hog or as the sequel to that game you needed to play DayZ back in the day. And even if you've read a review, some of my favorite features are new since it was released, including my favorite thing in gaming, Zeus mode. So in honor of it still being on sale for one more day, let me tell you why you should be playing ARMA 3 in 2017.

ARMA 3 is a FPS focused on a realistic scale, near-future vehicles and equipment, and flexibility for large-scale fights with combined arms. It allows high player counts for multiplayer, it's got a healthy modding community, it's maintained by an active development team that basically does nothing else, and it has a dedication to realism that makes other games seem goofy. And they to this day only have male character models, so they aren't concerned about getting the SJW vote at the expense of development time for their actual players.

Before I go any futher, some videos: Shacktac 2015 year in review, or the 2016 version which I like less. The 2015 edition does have some footage from ARMA 2 too. These videos are highlights of what the game is like for large scale servers with not many mods, actual play can differ hugely.

Or here are the trailers for the American and Russian factions from the RHS mod if you're concerned about the "near future" gear in the default game.

The scale: The game comes with two maps- the islands of Altis and Stratis, both based on real Greek islands. They're big enough that I'd hate to have to drive across Altis, let alone walk. So there's no problem with hitting the edge of the map. Objectives can be pretty much any distance apart, so if you want to have a two-hour long patrol by foot, or a half-hour cruise by jeep, the map will let you do it if that's the sort of mission you want, and give you plenty of horizon to watch for threats. Which you'd better do, because 300 meters is close range in this game. If you can see someone easily, you're already close enough you should probably be in cover. 600m is still in the danger zone, and some rifles are a threat beyond 1km, depending on various factors. So managing which guns are available makes a significant difference how the combat feels and what range it happens at.

With this scale comes a different pace. Room clearing and urban combat is more like various Battlefield games, but out in the country, ARMA is special. There are probably bad guys around, and you definitely need to keep an eye open, but you're probably safe any given instant. It's like taking a walk in the country, with the possibility that the next hill have a bunch of people who will murder you if you don't see them first. It also allows a ton of flexibility for how you approach any objective- ARMA is the opposite of a corridor shooter. You can go straight at them, you can take the low ground to avoid exposure, you can take the high ground to have good visibility, you can grab a vehicle, do an air drop, you can really use your brain to decide exactly how you're going to do things, because you don't need to worry about some bullshit "Leaving mission area" message popping up when you try to get a little creative about your approach.

The flexibility: ARMA has a campaign, and it actually does a pretty okay job of gradually introducing you to what ARMA has to offer, but if you play ARMA, it's probably for content made by someone else, or that you make yourself. Missions, mods that turn the game into some kind of "alternate life RPG", a zombie game mode, scenarios that indefinitely generate random objectives, there's a lot of stuff to play, but the most powerful two factors are the editor and Zeus mode. The editor now has a 3D mode, which lets you see the actual stuff you're putting down in real time, making the barrier to entry trivial. But better than that is...

Zeus mode: introduced well after the game came out, it's basically dungeon master mode. You're an eye in the sky, and you've got a menu on the right with every object in the game, from riflemen to complete buildings to airstrikes, that you can spawn at will around the people playing. You can build missions on the fly and react to the decisions your players make in real time. Give orders to the AI or take direct control of any AI on the map, which is still fun solo- spawn some guys, take control of one of them, and play the scenario you just made.

Realism: It has nine different stances, not counting leans and step right/step left, just to put things in perspective. A velocity/bullet drop/penetration model which is better than anything I'm aware of outside of a dedicated sniping game, and really differentiates different calibers. Getting shot is bad for your health. Combined arms are real.

Community: There are a lot of groups that play ARMA in different ways, and some of them will take new players right away if you just show up to their play sessions. There are also servers running randomly generated missions 24 hours a day for getting your feet wet, or any number of mods to try and groups to join. I worked my way up from rifleman to team leader to squad leader on a vanilla server run by someone who knew what he was doing, and it was a fairly fascinating learning experience.

Performance: Really not as bad as you've heard! Partially because hardware has moved on since it's been released, and partially because there have been several patches focused on it. I'm running a 4690K / 970, and I am often capped at 60, and only drop below 30 when things are pretty serious.

The sound should get it's own mention- in the marksman update, they revamped the sound to separate the sound of a gun firing and the sound of a bullet. So you get the separate whip crack of a bullet, followed by the bang of the gun, separated by the speed of sound difference. It sounds small, but it really does contribute to feeling like it's real.

New stuff since release: Zeus mode, 3D editor mode, gun sounds as above, slingloading helicopters, tentative Linux support, the arsenal which makes managing loadouts hugely better than the goddamn nightmare it was previously, a bipod/deployment system for bracing weapons, an advanced flight model for helicopters, 64 bit support.

DLC: Mostly not a big deal, because they always add any new core gameplay mechanics to the main game as well. The Kart DLC is basically an April Fools joke made real; the Marksman DLC has a few new guns that fill slightly different roles but aren't critical; the helicopter DLC adds a couple new helicopters; but the Tanoa DLC adds a new, tropical island, the equivalent of a VTOL C130 gunship, another VTOL, a bunch of new guns, I think a couple of land vehicles, and probably some stuff I'm forgetting.

The downside: Some of the complaints about ARMA are legitimate. The AI is entirely general purpose, so sometimes it does things that don't make sense, and can be very reluctant to advance under fire, for instance. There are various AI mods that improve or change behaviour or make them less lethal shooters if you want that. There can be player movement issues. There's a "big step" key that can usually get you out of whatever you're stuck inside, but occasionally you'll take damage from accidentally phasing through a rock or something. Some of the sounds can be imperfect. I hear your framerate can be negatively affected by the server's own speed, though I haven't really looked into that.

Here's a link to some previous stuff I wrote about ARMA 3, covering some of the stuff a new player might want to do.

And lastly, I'm always looking for new players to play Zeus with.
